B000490.text: This week, the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, appeared before the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government. During the hearing, I asked the Director about how Congress can be any clearer to ensure that the Trump Administration understands that once a funding bill is signed into law, the President is not allowed to change or second-guess the spending and withhold it due to policy or political differences. That is at the heart of Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution and why Congress also passed the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, when President Nixon tried to withhold funds that were already obligated according to the law.

This week, I asked the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, to explain how poorly planned cuts to the federal workforce last year have weakened services and protections upon which Americans rely. This includes the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which is responsible for protecting America’s agriculture from invasive species and diseases. USDA-APHIS began mounting a vigorous response to the resurgence of New World Screwworm – a deadly parasite affecting livestock – in 2024. However, in early 2025, the Administration illegally fired workers and forced others to resign, causing over 25 percent of all USDA-APHIS employees to leave. USDA’s New World Screwworm prevention, monitoring, surveillance, and control efforts were halted. USDA had approved $378 million in prevention and control funding for sterile fly facilities in 2023 and 2024, yet the money went unspent when the new administration paused funding. This is extremely concerning to our ranchers, and this outbreak could drive the price of food even higher. Unfortunately, we continue to see the fallout of the blunt and ill-considered cuts to federal workers, from the return of New World Screwworm to the United States, to farmers showing up to closed or understaffed Farm Service Agency offices, to attacks on our nuclear safety programs putting national security at risk. C001053.text: There are few corners of Capitol Hill where South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham wasn't known. Whether you knew him personally or simply watched him at work, he was impossible to ignore.   Lindsey was a ubiquitous presence in Washington – with few office holders as visible, quotable, or energetic as him. For more than three decades, he served throughout the House and Senate – building a reputation as a determined legislator, a media presence, and a dealmaker. From the green rooms to the global stage, Lindsey was always in the middle of the debate, making the case for what he believed in for South Carolina and the nation.   When it came to foreign affairs, Graham was an old-fashioned statesman and hawk. He believed America was a force for good in the world, and he never hesitated to confront those who threatened our interests and our allies – from Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea to terrorist organizations around the globe.   As Appropriators serving in different chambers, we worked together and shared a commitment to a strong national defense. I always appreciated his insight, his candor, and his willingness to pick up the phone to exchange ideas, discuss Oklahoma figures or issues, or strategize how we could bridge differences between the House and Senate. He was never shy about calling to seek advice, compare notes, or test his own impressions – a quality that reflected both his confidence and his respect for the views of others.   Lindsey approached public service with boundless energy, sharp wit, and genuine optimism. He loved serving in Congress, and it showed every day. He was a gifted communicator, a persuasive advocate, and someone who never lost his enthusiasm for the institution or for the work of governing.   I will miss Senator Lindsey Graham, and so will the Congress he served so faithfully. His gregarious nature always left us with points made crispy, cleanly, and with a laugh. That energy and humor certainly made him the ‘happy warrior’ of his political generation. His leadership, collegiality, and unmistakable presence will be deeply missed.

Terrorists. Cartels. Human traffickers. Drug smugglers. Each day, ICE and Border Patrol agents and officers confront these threats head-on to keep America safe. It’s exactly why I have consistently voted to comprehensively resource these law enforcement professionals as they carry out their security missions. While the far-left hoped to eradicate funding for critical operations and weaken our border security apparatus, House Republicans have made clear that we will continue to support those who defend our homeland and keep our communities safe. That's why we passed the Secure America Act today. However, while I do not regret the objective of our actions today, I am appalled by the complete failure of Senate Democrats that led us to this moment. Chuck Schumer and his radical caucus twice shut down the government, instigating chaos across the nation. Since then, they have continued to diminish Article I and forced the use of reconciliation. It’s wrong – and deliberately undermines the appropriations process. The Constitution entrusts Congress with the power of the purse. Yet, in great irony, the Senate has shown greater concern for protecting an internal rule than fulfilling its constitutional duty. The filibuster is nothing more than an institutional habit. It is neither mentioned nor sanctioned in our founding documents. I would remind my peers on the other side of the Rotunda that no chamber precedent is greater than the bedrock of our Republic. Members swear an oath to uphold the Constitution – not the filibuster. I thoroughly regret the erosion of Article I authority that Senate Democrats have instigated, and the price everyday Americans have been forced to pay as a result. I hope the months-long charade that led us to this moment serves as a reminder that no partisan fixation is worth shutting down the government, abandoning constitutional responsibilities, and forcing Congress into extraordinary measures simply to perform its most basic duties. I believe in the Constitution, the power of the purse, and completing the appropriations process. I also believe in keeping the homeland safe. The Senate may have abandoned proper governing, but I will not abandon those who stand watch over our borders and protect our communities. Our work, of course, doesn’t end here. As the Fiscal Year 2027 Appropriations markups near completion, I am reminded that governing is a choice. The work I do, the votes I cast, and the actions I take will always be guided by one principle: fulfilling our obligations to the American people

C000880.text: For most of my public service in Congress, I had the privilege of calling Lindsey Graham not only a colleague in both the House and Senate, but a loyal and generous friend. He was a formidable public servant who held the line on issues important to him and South Carolinians with unwavering courage. As an Air Force veteran and foreign policy hawk, he traveled the world demonstrating America’s strength and resolve. To our nation’s allies, he was a friend. To our adversaries, he was unflinching. This afternoon, while in Duval County alongside County Judge Arnold Cantu, County Sheriff Romeo Ramirez, County Clerk Sally Lichtenberger, and the Commissioners' Court, I announced $170,000 in federal funding I secured through the FY2025 Operation Stonegarden Grant Program for the Duval County Sheriff's Office. I helped create Operation Stonegarden because I knew our border communities needed a reliable federal partnership to support local law enforcement. Since Duval County joined the program in 2018, it has received more than $1.4 million to help cover personnel, equipment, supplies, and other operational costs. These federal dollars will help fund overtime for deputies, expand law enforcement coverage, strengthen public safety across Duval County, and ensure local officers have the resources they need to continue protecting our communities.

Today, alongside Zapata County Judge Joe Rathmell, Justice of the Peace Olga Bruni, Zapata County Sheriff Ramon Montes, and Commissioner Joey Solis, I announced $293,070 in federal funding I secured through the FY2025 Operation Stonegarden Grant Program for the Zapata County Sheriff's Office. As the original author of Operation Stonegarden, I've continued fighting to ensure our border communities have the resources they need to keep families safe. Since the program's creation, Zapata County has received more than $10.3 million through Operation Stonegarden to support local law enforcement. This funding will support overtime for local deputies, strengthen law enforcement efforts, enhance public safety across Zapata County, and allow the Sheriff's Office to purchase brand-new patrol units, helping improve emergency response capabilities throughout the county.

This morning, I announced $25 million in federal dollars I secured through the U.S. Department of Transportation's BUILD Grant Program for the City of Laredo's World Trade Bridge Expansion Project. This investment will help add two new lanes to the existing bridge and construct a new eight-lane northbound commercial bridge, increasing capacity, reducing congestion, and keeping goods moving more efficiently through our nation's busiest commercial port of entry. Today's announcement builds on my continued efforts to secure federal investments for Laredo's international bridges. In addition to this $25 million BUILD Grant, I've helped secure a $62 million renovation project for Bridge II and a $27 million renovation project for Bridge I in 2015, ensuring our ports of entry remain competitive and prepared for continued growth. Thank you to Mayor Dr. Victor Treviño, the City of Laredo, and all of our partners who helped make this project possible. I'll continue working to bring federal investments home and ensure South Texas has the infrastructure it needs to support jobs, strengthen our supply chain, and keep American trade moving. Together, we're continuing to strengthen Laredo's position as the nation's #1 inland port.

For 250 years, our great experiment has faltered, flourished, evolved, and progressed. The American experience is ever-changing and as diverse as the people who call this country home. But one thing has remained constant – the idea of America has always been a beacon of hope. Protecting this country and the ideals and values it was founded on takes work. Democracy is demanding. It takes dedication and principle. And it takes the resounding belief that upholding those ideals and values is worth the fight because America is bigger than any one person. Because liberty can only truly endure when it is paired with responsibility, virtue, and a commitment to put public good ahead of personal ambition. Today, we celebrate the moment when our founding fathers openly declared that creating this country, based in liberty, was a necessity in the face of tyranny. Their legacy is that leadership requires courage when it’s difficult, integrity when no one is watching, and a willingness to put country above self. We must remember that our duty is not merely to the next election, but to the next generation. That should be the challenge for all Americans as we look forward to another 250 years. From Massachusetts, where the fight for freedom first began, I wish you a happy 4th of July. God Bless America always, God Bless all who call her home, and God Bless our courageous men and women in uniform who continue the fight for liberty today.

On Monday, our office suffered an unimaginable loss. Chris Matthews, my District Outreach and Communications Director, passed away unexpectedly. If any one of you begin to lose faith in our country, remember Chris Matthews. Remember he was without question one of the Commonwealth’s sharpest political minds – a generational talent. Remember that he was more than a Congressional aide. He took the belief that through our actions we all can bring needed change and brought it with him on many interstate bus rides to canvas distant pivotal states and to the doors of the families he inspired. Remember through his example that public service is a genuinely noble vocation. As a trusted member of our office, he helped countless veterans, families, and those who could not advocate for themselves. Those of us privileged to have worked with him for over fifteen years will remember his laugh and his wry, often biting, humor – contrasting the way things are to the way they could be. We will always remember his authentic belief that in this country, people can bring about progress and meaningful change. It was real to him and his sincerity shown through. Chris was a genuinely good person. He was family to all of us, and we are devastated by his loss, particularly at such a young age. Our thoughts and prayers are with Molly and Eli and the many who loved him. Though we wish we had more time with him, his memory will continue to give us faith that one person can significantly make better the lives of those around him.

The Supreme Court’s decision today recognizes that states face unique circumstances in administering their elections. In Alaska, voting is not as simple as driving down the road to a neighborhood polling place. Many Alaskans live in remote communities that are not connected to the road system, requiring ballots to travel by bush plane or boat, which means volatile weather conditions and limited infrastructure can determine whether those ballots arrive on time. Pinned: The news of Senator Lindsey Graham’s passing saddens me deeply. Lindsey was one of America’s fiercest champions for freedom, democracy, and peace through strength. He carried forward the legacy of Senator John McCain, believing America’s leadership is indispensable and that nations seeking freedom should never stand alone. Lindsey was also a personal mentor. His counsel shaped my work in Congress, and despite his many responsibilities, he always made time to help others. I saw that firsthand when preparing for the 2025 NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Dayton. The summit welcomed more than 2,500 delegates from across the Alliance, and it would not have been possible without Lindsey’s personal intervention and support. That generosity toward fellow members was simply who he was. Just days ago, I had the honor of standing beside Lindsey in Ankara as we met with President Zelenskyy. Until his final days, he was pressing the case for stronger sanctions against Russia. There is no better way to honor his final mission than for the Senate and the White House to swiftly send his bipartisan Russia sanctions legislation to the President’s desk. Lindsey believed America must stand with nations seeking democracy because doing so strengthens our own security. We owe it to his legacy to ensure that commitment remains the foundation of American foreign policy. My prayers are with Lindsey’s family, his staff, the people of South Carolina, and all who knew him. America has lost a great statesman, and I have lost a mentor. His legacy will endure wherever freedom is defended. @LindseyGrahamSC

Arkansas, and the United States, have an incredibly abundant source of timber. Unfortunately, we look to nations outside of our borders to supply us with a resource that we have right here in our own back yard. Healthy forest management is more than just taking care of our trees, in fact we have been loving our trees to death. Our forests are overstocked and unhealthy because we have no markets for the wood and rural communities are suffering because their resource and economic opportunity are tied directly to the forests. A nation with such an abundance of timber should never be reliant on other countries to import lumber and pulp products, but that’s where we find ourselves.  Recently, we’ve seen paper mills across the country closing – even a few here in the Fourth District. With a background in Forestry and Engineering, Congressman Westerman understands just how important our pulp and paper industry is and he remains heavily focused on legislation that will support such an important economic contributer for Arkansas. This week’s meeting with the Pulp & Paperworkers’ Resource Council to discuss just how important the forest products industry underscored the need for Congress to work diligently to provide its support.

S001198.text: Julie and I are shocked and heartbroken about the sudden passing of Lindsey Graham. He was a dear friend and colleague, a patriot, a veteran, and a staunch advocate for his state, for his party, and for our country’s national security. He was one of a kind—witty and wise, a true friend, and one of our nation’s most important and influential U.S. Senators. It was an honor to laugh with him and learn from him. For Alaskans, the decades-long King Cove Road impasse has been a symbol of an uncaring, out-of-touch, faraway federal government that prioritizes the lives of birds over people. I’ve been working with the people of King Cove on this issue back to my time as Alaska’s Commissioner of the Department of Natural Resources through my time serving as U.S. Senator. Time and again these great Alaskans have kept hope alive, despite setbacks, most recently when the Biden administration disregarded the voices of the community and withdrew the previously approved land exchange. The permit issued by the Corps of Engineers today is vindication for King Cove, putting us closer than ever before to delivering a lifesaving, 11-mile, single-lane gravel road to the all-weather airport in Cold Bay. I want to thank the Administration, especially Secretary Burgum and Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works Telle, for listening to Alaskans, for caring about their safety and well-being, and for putting us on the cusp of a historic breakthrough for safe and reliable access for King Cove.

Last week, I had the opportunity to welcome @USDOTFHWA Sean McMaster to Alaska to see firsthand our state’s critical infrastructures needs and to hear from Alaskans about how the federal government can work better with all our stakeholders to expedite the delivery of these projects. First steel was being cut on our new Arctic Security Cutter months before the contract was even finalized! That’s the kind of initiative and urgency we need to build these new icebreakers and close the gap we face with our adversaries in the Arctic. With three of these new icebreakers being homeported right here in Alaska—in addition to the Storis in Juneau—we’re building a strong foundation for America’s Arctic Security future!

Last week, at the Port of Alaska groundbreaking ceremony, I mentioned the pressure my team and I have put on federal agency heads to resolve a decade-long lawsuit over port funding. Yesterday, a settlement was finally announced, unlocking $191 million to go directly toward construction and building on the hundreds of millions of federal dollars my congressional delegation colleagues and I have secured for the project over the years. The funding we’ve secured for the port is critically important for Alaska, first, because it will lower the cost of living for Alaska’s hard-working families—everything from energy to groceries. The port modernization is also vital for supporting the renaissance of energy development happening on the North Slope and the future build-out of the Alaska LNG project. Finally, the Port of Alaska is very important to U.S. national security and the military build-up taking place in our state, especially the historic $7 billion ‘Fighter Town’ recapitalization coming to JBER. I will continue pressing for the funding needed to complete this project and bringing up top federal officials—like the U.S. Attorney General, the U.S. Transportation Secretary, the MARAD Administrator, and the USTRANSCOM Commander—so they understand and appreciate how important this piece of infrastructure is for Alaska and for America.

R000605.text: Saddened by the sudden loss of my friend Lindsey Graham. He was a public servant who cared deeply for South Carolina and the people he served. Lindsey was also a foreign policy hawk and a friend to our allies around the world. He had a significant role in navigating some of the most serious conflicts of our time. He shepherded several conservative justices through the Judiciary committee as chairman. More recently, his work as Budget chairman paved the way for our reconciliation packages over the past couple of years. Lindsey’s work in the Senate was influential and will be felt by Americans for decades to come. While he was a statesman, I’ll remember Lindsey as a friend. Personally, he was funny, thoughtful and headstrong. Throughout it all, he never lost his wit. I’ll always remember that about him. America lost a good public servant, and I lost a good friend. There are some people you are simply grateful to have known. Tom Yaegel of Richboro was one of them. He was a veteran, patriot, builder, mentor, and a man whose life touched far more people than he probably ever knew—a true Hometown Hero. I was proud to call him a friend, and will always remember his quick wit, larger-than-life presence, relentless drive, and the deep love he had for his family, community, and country. Tom answered America’s call during the Vietnam War, earning his commission through Officer Candidate School and serving in the Army Corps of Engineers in support of U.S. Special Forces. When he came home, he built a life with the same grit and determination he brought to his service. For 56 years, he shared that life with his beloved wife, Ann. He built a family he adored, businesses that became local institutions, and opportunities that changed lives. Through the Richboro Swim Club and Valley of Fear, Tom created more than places people visited. He created places people remember. Generations of families spent their summers there. Generations of young people got their first jobs there. Friendships began there. Traditions took root there. And so many people learned from Tom that hard work, responsibility, loyalty, and doing right by others still matter. That is the kind of legacy that lasts. As our great nation continues to mark 250 years, Tom’s life is a reminder that the strength of this country has always come from people like him—Americans who serve when called, create opportunity, invest and uplift others, and leave their communities stronger than they found them. Tom did all of that. May we keep Ann, his children, grandchildren, the entire Yaegel family, and all who knew and loved Tom in our prayers. Our community is better because of him, and his legacy will live on here forever.

John Adams called Independence Day America’s “Day of Deliverance.” The Declaration of Independence - that sacred parchment - is the cornerstone of American exceptionalism and the foundation for the longest-sustained constitutional democracy in the world. It affirms the birthright of every American citizen: our God-given rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. The Declaration of Independence wasn’t just a list of grievances; it was a treatise on man and his natural rights - a mission statement for how such men should be governed. No one at the time gave us a fighting chance of defeating the world’s superpower for our independence. And few predicted we’d persist for a quarter of a millennium. Our founding visionaries weren’t sure of either outcome themselves, but they believed in our inherent rights and God-given freedoms and would rather die fighting for them than live under tyranny. They trusted in “divine Providence” for protection and mutually pledged to each other “our Lives, our Fortunes and our sacred Honor.” They held fast to truth, they stood firm for justice, and they fought like warrior poets for our freedom. And, by the grace of Almighty God, our revolutionary ancestors gave birth to the most powerful and prosperous nation in human history. Let’s honor their vision, courage, and conviction by solemnly dedicating ourselves to preserving this “Great Experiment” in liberty and self-government. Happy 250th Independence Day to all my God-fearing, freedom-loving American patriots! May God continue to have mercy upon and give favor to our beloved nation. U-S-A, U-S-A…!! Your proud US Representative and fellow West Texan, Jodey

Fun Fact Friday: As we celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, I want to highlight some of the signers of the Declaration of Independence. Thomas Lynch was born in South Carolina in 1749. He spent several years in England studying and meeting with many English politicians. Upon hearing about the unrest in the colonies, he traveled back to America. His father had been elected to serve in the Continental Congress, but his father’s health was failing. Therefore, Thomas came in and served alongside his father. Thomas signed the Declaration but his father’s health issues prevented him from signing the document before his death. Thomas and his wife passed away in 1779, when the ship he and his wife were traveling on disappeared into the Bermuda Triangle.

T000480.text: Over the last decade, I had the privilege of knowing Lindsey Graham not just as a United States Senator, but as a mentor, a travel companion, a golf partner, and, most importantly, a friend. We traveled together on congressional delegation trips around the world, spent countless hours talking about politics, life, South Carolina, and played what had to be close to 100 rounds of golf together. Some of my favorite memories weren't in Congress—they were walking fairways, talking through the issues of the day, and enjoying a game he truly loved. We even had a standing rule: if a world leader called while we were playing, Lindsey could answer the phone and I'd automatically give him a par. It happened more than you'd think. Calls from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, President Donald Trump, or President Volodymyr Zelenskyy weren't unusual. Somehow, Lindsey could seamlessly transition from discussing the most consequential issues in the world to reading a putt and asking whether I thought it broke left or right. One memory I'll treasure forever is when I was the only person fortunate enough to witness Lindsey make a double eagle on the 9th hole at his beloved Cliffs at Mountain Park. Anyone who knew him knows that was one of the proudest moments of his golfing life. For all that Lindsey accomplished, what always impressed me most was where he came from. He was the embodiment of the American dream. After losing both of his parents as a young man, Lindsey made the extraordinary decision to raise his younger sister, Darline. He often spoke about how survivor Social Security benefits helped the two of them make it through those unimaginably difficult years. He never forgot where he came from, and he never forgot the responsibility he carried. Long before the Senate, he was working in his family's liquor store and pool hall in Central, South Carolina. Those experiences shaped the way he saw the world. He could relate just as easily to a mechanic, a waitress, or a soldier as he could to a president or prime minister because he had lived a life that looked a lot more like theirs than Washington's. His service to our country extended far beyond Congress. Lindsey proudly served for more than three decades in the Air Force and Air Force Reserves, ultimately attaining the rank of colonel. President George W. Bush personally officiated his promotion ceremony to full bird colonel, an honor that reflected the respect he had earned through decades of military service. As someone who also wears the uniform, I was fortunate to have Lindsey as a mentor there as well. He taught me that public service does not begin or end with elected office, but that it is a lifelong commitment to something greater than yourself. Lindsey was a fierce advocate for South Carolina and for America, but those of us who knew him personally will remember something even more important. He was loyal. He invested in people. He gave candid advice, expected your best, celebrated your successes, and picked you up after your failures. He made countless people better simply because they had the privilege of knowing him. My heart is with his extraordinary staff, who stood beside him through every challenge and every victory, and especially with his beloved sister, Darline, who was always at the center of his life. I will miss the golf, the conversations, the advice, the laughter, and yes—even the phone ringing in the middle of a round because another world leader needed Lindsey Graham. Thank you for your friendship, your mentorship, and your example. Rest easy, my friend. South Carolina—and our nation—are far better because you were here.

On this day in history, in 1804 in New Jersey, Aaron Burr mortally wounds Alexander Hamilton in a duel. Aaron Burr, who was the third Vice President at the time, and Alexander Hamilton, the first and previous Secretary of the Treasury, had a rivalry for many years. The duel was the result of Hamilton referring to Burr as a “dangerous man” in a published newspaper article. Although the witnesses turned around before shots were fired since duels were illegal in New Jersey, it’s believed that Hamilton shot into the air while Burr fired at Hamilton’s hip. Hamilton died the next day. Burr was charged with murder in New York and New Jersey, but his allies had the charges dropped. He finished out his term as Vice President, which marked the end of his political career.

On this day in history in 1985, France’s foreign intelligence agency bombed the Greenpeace flagship Rainbow Warrior in New Zealand’s Auckland Harbor. The ship was preparing to lead a protest against French nuclear testing in the Pacific when two French agents planted explosives onboard, killing a photographer. France initially denied involvement, but after the agents were captured, the government admitted responsibility.

On this day in history in 1795, James Swan paid off the entire U.S. national debt of $2,024,899. A Boston patriot and member of the Sons of Liberty, Swan bought the U.S. debt to France and sold it as interest-bearing shares to private investors. This move shifted America’s debt from foreign governments to private hands, strengthening the young nation’s financial footing.

One year ago today, on the Fourth of July, our nation celebrated the blessings of freedom while families across Texas experienced unimaginable heartbreak. We pause today to remember every precious life lost at Camp Mystic and every other life taken far too soon in that tragedy. We remember the children whose futures were just beginning, the counselors and adults who stood courageously in harm’s way, and every family whose lives were forever changed. Their names, their stories, and their memories will never be forgotten. No words can truly ease the pain of such profound loss. Yet even in the darkest moments, we witnessed the very best of America. To every law enforcement officer, firefighter, EMS professional, dispatcher, game warden, pilot, medic, search-and-rescue specialist, and every first responder who answered the call, thank you. You ran toward danger while others were running away. You worked through exhaustion, heartbreak, and impossible conditions with courage, professionalism, and compassion. Your service honored every life you were fighting to save. To the countless volunteers who showed up without being asked—neighbors, veterans, church groups, ranchers, boat owners, businesses, families, and complete strangers—you reminded us that the strength of our communities is measured not only by what we say, but by what we do. You brought supplies, comfort, equipment, prayers, and hope. You asked for nothing in return except the opportunity to help another human being. That spirit defines Texas. As we remember those we lost, let us also remember the enduring responsibility we share: to love our neighbors, to care for those who grieve, and to ensure that the memories of these lives continue to inspire acts of kindness, service, and sacrifice. Finally, I want to offer my deepest gratitude to the men of the BEARKAT team. There are simply no words sufficient to express what you endured or what you accomplished. You answered a calling that demanded extraordinary courage, unwavering resolve, and selfless service. You carried burdens that few will ever fully understand, and you did so with quiet professionalism and humility. It is impossible to thank you enough for all that you did. Your actions brought comfort to grieving families, hope in moments of despair, and honor to everyone you represent. Texas will forever be grateful, and your service will never be forgotten. May we always remember those we lost, honor those who served, and carry forward the enduring truth that even in our darkest hours, courage, compassion, and faith will always light the way.

J000311.text: Today, we mourn the passing of United States Senator Lindsey Graham, a fierce advocate for the people of South Carolina.  May his memory be a blessing to his family and friends. Born in Upstate South Carolina, tragedy struck Lindsey early in his life.  After he graduated from high school, Lindsey’s mother and father passed away within 15 months of each other, leaving him without parents and his 13-year-old sister orphaned.  Lindsey shifted his focus to raising and caring for his sister, assuming a responsibility few can imagine at that age. The resilience and sense of duty he developed during those difficult years would come to define a lifetime of service. For 33 years, Lindsey served our Country in the United States Air Force.  He was awarded the Bronze Star for meritorious service shortly before retiring as a Colonel. For 31 years, Lindsey served in the United States Congress, and became one of the most influential lawmakers in our Country. Lindsey’s unexpected passing also affirms a profound truth: every day we live is a gift and a blessing from God.

As of Monday morning, several thousand residents of the Lehigh Valley and the Poconos continue to lack power. Here’s what you need to know: ⚡ Avoid downed power lines. If you live in PPL’s service area and encounter a downed line, please call 1-800-342-5775 and say "downed power line." 📅 Know the schedule. While most local residents have had their power restored, some of those impacted by more complex outages remain without power. PPL anticipates that power will be restored to all areas by Wednesday, July 8th, with many seeing earlier restorations. ℹ️ Stay informed. Get updates, report outages, and see the latest map by visiting https://stories.pplelectric.com/storm-updates/ 💵 Keep receipts for ice and gallons of water. PPL is offering reimbursement for up to three 10lb bags of ice and three gallons of water per day for those impacted. Thank you to the local lineworkers who are working around the clock to restore power to our community.

WORLD_FRANCE_PRESIDENT.text: Son Altesse l’Emir–Père, Cheikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al–Thani, s’est éteint aujourd’hui. J’adresse à Son Altesse Cheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al–Thani, à sa famille et au peuple qatarien toutes mes condoléances et l’assurance de mon amitié et de celle du peuple français. Cheikh Hamad a vécu en géant, il devient aujourd’hui une légende. Homme visionnaire au service des aspirations de son peuple, il a été l’artisan inlassable de la modernisation spectaculaire du Qatar dans tous les domaines et a fait de son pays un acteur mondialement reconnu et respecté. Tout au long de son règne, Cheikh Hamad s’est attaché à construire une relation forte et confiante avec la France, au service d’une vision partagée des grands enjeux régionaux et internationaux. Fidèle à cet héritage, je réaffirme à mon ami Cheikh Tamim ma détermination à œuvrer avec lui à l’approfondissement continu du partenariat stratégique qui unit nos deux pays.
Le Dreyfusisme nous rappelle que l’antisémitisme, quelle qu’en soit la racine ou les explications prétendues, est l’ennemi de la République.

Le 12 juillet 1906, la plus haute juridiction de notre pays proclamait l'innocence du capitaine Alfred Dreyfus. Triomphe de la justice après des années de combat et le lent dévoilement de la vérité. Mais ce que Dreyfus et les dreyfusards ont légué à la France dépasse le sort d'un seul homme. Tous ont démontré que si une nation peut se déchirer sur le destin d’un simple capitaine, elle peut aussi, grâce à la vigilance et la persévérance des Hommes de bonne volonté, choisir la Vérité et la Justice. Chaque 12 juillet, désormais, nous nous souviendrons de cela : que la justice et la vérité ont vaincu la haine et le mensonge, et qu'elles doivent, chaque jour, être défendues à nouveau.

9 départs de feu sur 10 sont dus à une activité humaine. Une seconde d’inattention peut menacer des familles, mettre en danger ceux qui nous protègent et détruire nos paysages. Chacun a une responsabilité. Soyons vigilants. À nos soldats du feu, gratitude et soutien.
